introduction-beyond-the-search-box.core: OpenSearch Service runs managed OpenSearch (an Elasticsearch fork) for full-text search, log analytics, observability and vector search. Data lives in indices split into shards distributed across data nodes. Production clusters need careful node roles, shard sizing, storage tiers and cross-cluster features.

first_principles.problem: A logging cluster with default settings goes red under load and costs a fortune in hot storage.

analogy.title: A library with a card catalogue, branches and archives
analogy.story: Fast lookups, books spread across branches and old volumes moved to cheaper storage.
analogy.breaks: Library catalogues are updated slowly; OpenSearch indexes thousands of documents per second.

flow: ISM: hot 7 d → UltraWarm 30 d → cold 1 y

the-brain-vs-the-body-dedicated-master-n.core: Cluster manager (master) nodes maintain cluster state (index metadata, shard allocation) and elect a leader; data nodes store and query shards. Dedicated masters (3, across AZs, for quorum) keep cluster management stable when data nodes are busy. Without them, heavy queries can starve state updates and cause split-brain or red clusters.

first_principles.problem: Under heavy indexing, the cluster becomes unresponsive and shards stop allocating.
truths: Cluster state must be managed reliably.
Quorum needs an odd number of voters.
Data work can starve management work.
derivation: Size masters by **shard and index count**.
Watch **cluster state size** and shard count.

analogy.title: A brain and a body
analogy.story: The body does heavy lifting; the brain coordinates and must not be exhausted by lifting too.
analogy.breaks: Brains can't be replaced; master nodes can, as long as quorum holds.

example.title: Stabilising a cluster
flow: Before: data nodes also master-eligible, frequent timeouts
Cluster state updates stable under load

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: No more red during ingest spikes.

check.q: Why use three dedicated master nodes?
check.a: An odd number maintains quorum for leader election and avoids split-brain, while dedicated nodes stay responsive.

the-storage-tiers-hot-warm-and-cold.core: Hot tier data nodes use fast local/EBS storage for active indexing and frequent queries. UltraWarm stores read-only indices on S3 with caching nodes, cutting cost by up to ~90%. Cold storage detaches indices entirely to S3 at the lowest cost, attaching them on demand. ISM policies move indices between tiers by age or size.

first_principles.problem: A year of logs on hot storage costs ten times what the queries justify.
truths: S3 is far cheaper than SSD.
Old logs are rarely queried but must be retained.

analogy.title: Kitchen counter, pantry and basement storage
analogy.story: Today's ingredients on the counter, this month's in the pantry and old preserves in the basement.
analogy.breaks: Basement items are fetched by hand; cold indices are attached through an API.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Storage cost drops by most of the bill.

check.q: Can you write to indices in UltraWarm?

deep-dive-how-ultrawarm-works.core: UltraWarm nodes keep index data in S3 and use local storage as a cache for frequently accessed segments. Queries fetch needed blocks from S3 into the cache, with prefetching. Indices must be read-only and are typically force-merged to fewer segments first. Performance is slower than hot for cold-cache queries but far cheaper.

first_principles.problem: Teams are surprised that the first query on an UltraWarm index is slow and later ones are fast.
truths: S3 has higher latency than local disk.
derivation: Size **UltraWarm nodes** for cache and concurrency.
Keep **dashboards** on hot where latency matters.

analogy.title: A library annex with a small reading-room shelf
analogy.story: Books live in the warehouse; recently requested ones sit on the reading-room shelf.
analogy.breaks: Librarians predict popular books; UltraWarm uses access patterns and prefetching.

check.q: Why force-merge an index before moving it to UltraWarm?
check.a: Fewer, larger segments mean fewer S3 fetches and better query performance.

cross-cluster-search-the-federation.core: Cross-cluster search lets a coordinating cluster query indices on connected remote clusters (e.g. per team, per region or per environment) in a single request, using connection aliases (remote:index). Data stays in place, isolation and scaling are per cluster, and searches federate across them.

first_principles.problem: Security analysts need to search logs from ten regional clusters at once.
truths: Moving all data to one cluster is costly.
derivation: Create **outbound connections** from the coordinating domain.

analogy.title: A federated library catalogue
analogy.story: Search once and see results from every branch without moving the books.
analogy.breaks: Library federations can be slow to sync; CCS queries live data on each request.

check.q: How do you refer to a remote index in cross-cluster search?
check.a: With the connection alias prefix, e.g. alias:index-name.

cross-cluster-replication-ccr.core: Cross-cluster replication copies indices from a leader cluster to follower clusters asynchronously, near real time. Followers are read-only, providing low-latency regional reads and a warm disaster-recovery copy. Auto-follow rules replicate new indices matching patterns automatically.

first_principles.problem: A search application needs fast reads in two regions and a standby if one region fails.
derivation: Start **replication** per index or **auto-follow** by pattern.
On DR, **stop replication** and promote follower to writable.

analogy.title: A newspaper's regional printing plants
analogy.story: Headquarters writes the edition; plants print local copies moments later.
analogy.breaks: Newspapers are read-only everywhere; promoted followers can become writable after DR.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Every new products index replicates to EU.
